questions.question: What does a single neuron in a neural network mechanically do?
options: It stores a copy of the entire training dataset
It multiplies inputs by learned weights, adds a bias, sums the result, and passes it through an activation function
It runs a SQL query against a database
It directly outputs the final prediction for the whole network
questions.explanation: A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, then applies an activation function to produce its output — this simple operation, repeated across many neurons and layers, is the basis of neural networks.

questions.question: Why is an activation function necessary in a neural network?
options: It saves memory by compressing the weights
Without a non-linear activation function, stacking multiple layers would be mathematically no different than having just one layer
It is only needed for the very last layer of a network
It speeds up the computer's internet connection
questions.explanation: Activation functions introduce non-linearity. Without them, no matter how many layers are stacked, the whole network would collapse into a single linear transformation, unable to model complex relationships.

questions.question: A team proposes adding more layers to a model to improve accuracy, citing 99% training accuracy but only 60% accuracy on new data. What is the most important question to ask?
options: Can we just add even more layers regardless of this result?
Is this overfitting rather than underfitting, and would adding more layers make that worse instead of better?
Why does the model need any layers at all?
Can we ignore the accuracy on new data entirely?
questions.explanation: A large gap between training accuracy (99%) and new-data accuracy (60%) is a classic sign of overfitting. Adding more layers/parameters would likely worsen overfitting rather than help, since the model already has more capacity than it can generalize well with.
